There's another reason why this is very significant that is overlooked in this article and others on the topic. This is part of the key to CATS--cheap access to space--because it facilitates the creation of value on orbit instead of sending it there.

CATS is commonly seen to be about manned space flight and finding the magic bullet technology to make a seat on a spacecraft as cheap as one on an airliner. But it's really about the logistics of doing things in space in a more general sense. There are, in fact, already cheap ways to put stuff in space but we haven't used them because the kinds of things we send to space are too 'precious'. Payload value is what dictates launch costs. It's expensive to get to space largely because the things we send to space tend to be very costly themselves and so need all kinds of extra measures to insure their safety. And so rockets are designed with a premise that 'failure is not an option' and include all kinds of redundant systems and extreme care in engineering and handling to insure that failures are as rare as possible. All this adds mass to a rocket, which means it has to be that much larger to accommodate a given amount of payload, which in turn makes it more complex and thus harder to insure that reliability, and so more measures have to be taken to compensate, and so on. It's a vicious cycle.

But in normal industry failure is, indeed, an option. It's expected. Any kind of production will normally produce some percentage of bad units and the production scheme is not designed to eliminate that completely--which is impossible--but to keep it at a tolerable minimum relative to the value of units produced. A tolerable yield relative to marginal costs. And in many industries this can be as high as a third or even half. In electric power production about a third of the electricity produced is lost in the grid itself, never reaching any users. Once Japanese manufacturers had only a 50% production yield for TFT color flat panel displays, and that was considered something no other companies in the world could match. Microprocessor production is usually pretty messy. Only a small number of units meet the ideal performance standards. So to ameliorate that high failure rate, they have a sliding scale of performance and a sliding scale of unit value. They're all coming off the same chip wafers but some test and pass at a high performance level, some pass at lower performance levels and are sold at a lower price, and some don't work at all.

Now, imagine if we used rockets the same way. A couple decades ago the company Space Systems Loral proposed a new launch system to support the ISS. They suggested that it was a waste of money to use expensive manned launch systems like the Shuttle to carry cheap stuff like food and water to the space station. The overhead of system reliability wasn't justified for cheap stuff worth so much less than the launch system carrying it. If a load of food is lost now and then, who cares? So they suggested creating a very simplified launch system for carrying cheap stuff that eliminated the redundancy of conventional rockets and could be mass produced. They assumed about a third rate of failure and instead of halting all launches every time a rocket failed, they would just assume that as a tolerable loss, do the work of improvement in-line, and just keep right on launching. Of course, if you're anticipating that a third of everything you launch blows up, you can't launch in conventional launch facilities. You need something that is not going to be damaged when these rockets blow up and not near people. So they developed a rocket to be launched in the water at sea. No special launch structures. You just put it in the water and have it float vertically and run a flight control tether to a command ship or platform--the same way Russian ships and submarines launch ICBMs. And so they called this rocket Aquarius and planned to have it mass fabricated in California and shipped to Hawaii for launch off the coast.

There are other kinds of systems like this, such as QuickLaunch, a light gas gun that sits in the open sea. It's intended to launch small numerous resilient payloads. Fragile things can't withstand the forces of, literally, being shot out of a cannon to space so this will never suit human passengers. But if you're just sending simple materials, like rocket fuel in bulk, that's fine.

So imagine if, instead of sending the hardware we want to put in space, we made it there. Instead of making some satellite here on Earth that has an intrinsic value as great as a whole automobile plant and sending it up whole, you made that satellite on orbit. Then all you need to launch to space is the refined materials and small commodity parts--stuff that's pretty cheap so you can use these cheap means of launch and if it gets blown up every now and then, no big deal. You just roll that into your overhead. So you can see why a 3D printer in space is a big deal. The more we figure out how to make out there, the cheaper doing things out there is. The real key to CATS--at least for everything but humans--isn't some magic bullet technology that makes space travel cheap. It's leveraging technologies of production and automation in space on reducing the value of payloads so we can apply this tolerable yield paradigm to launch technology we already have.

And if we ever realize sentient AI and they decide to go to space, well, they're going to use this tolerable yield paradigm. They can travel by telecommunications instead of rockets so all they have to do is get the hardware to host them out there as cheaply as possible. So they will use this paradigm to beat us to every corner of the solar system and beyond.
